entries.title: CPU envelope: no software HiAE fallback
entries.c_behavior: HiAE is compiled from the amalgamated C source, which falls back to a table-based software AES when the CPU lacks AES instructions, so the program runs on any CPU.
entries.rust_behavior: HiAE comes from Graviola, which needs AES and carry-less multiply support (AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ on x86-64; AES and PMULL on AArch64). HiAeCipher::new checks the CPU after the key is loaded and, on a CPU below that baseline, the binary prints `twice: this CPU is not supported: HiAE needs ... CPU support` to stderr and exits 1 before it creates the TUN device. On every supported CPU the reproducer behaves identically to C, which is what the replay shows.

source_evidence.contains: this CPU is not supported: HiAE needs

entries.requires: a CPU below the Graviola baseline, such as QEMU qemu64 on x86-64; this host cannot show the failing side, so the reproducer proves only the supported-CPU agreement

entries.title: Public zero-key mode
entries.c_behavior: Without -k the program loads an all-zero key and authenticates each datagram with HiAE_mac under that public key. Payloads are cleartext and anybody who knows the protocol can compute a valid tag, so the tag provides no authentication against an attacker.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: Fixed-nonce keyed MTU probes
entries.c_behavior: Every MTU probe uses the constant header ffffffffffffffff ffffffffffffffff as its HiAE nonce, with the real key and a constant 0xAA plaintext. Same-size probes (retries, rediscovery after reconnect) encrypt to identical datagrams under one key and nonce, and the nonce is never one a normal data packet uses.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: Unauthenticated probe reflection
entries.c_behavior: The server checks for the probe magic header before it authenticates. Any datagram of at least 16 bytes that begins with sixteen 0xff bytes is sent back unchanged to its source address, up to the 65,568-byte receive buffer, with no key, tag, or session needed.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: Replay-driven peer address change
entries.c_behavior: After a datagram authenticates, the server stores its source as the client address before the reorder stage looks at the counter. A captured datagram replayed from another address, even a duplicate that the reorder stage then drops, redirects every later server-to-client packet to the replaying address.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: Replayed old-epoch reset
entries.c_behavior: A changed random value resets the reorder state and accepts the packet's counter. Replaying a captured datagram from an earlier epoch therefore resets state and delivers the replayed payload to the TUN device again, and the next real packet resets it back.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.
evidence: Random value mismatch - peer restarted. Resetting reorder state.

entries.title: Remote client reconnect on a bad datagram
entries.c_behavior: The client treats a 16 to 31 byte datagram, or one whose tag fails, as fatal for the session: it logs, closes the socket and reconnects. The connected UDP socket accepts any datagram whose source address is the server's, so an attacker who can spoof that address can force reconnects, each with a sleep ladder and a firewall pass, using one short datagram.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: Non-atomic genkey permissions
entries.c_behavior: genkey checks access(F_OK), creates the file with fopen("wb") and the process umask, writes the key, closes it, and only then calls chmod(0600). Between create and chmod the key file is readable under the umask, and the existence check races with creation. The shim shows the final 0600 mode, not the interval.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.

entries.title: atoi overflow in -m
entries.c_behavior: -m is parsed with atoi, whose overflow behavior ISO C leaves undefined. On the glibc oracle it is strtol saturating at LONG_MAX and LONG_MIN and then truncating to 32 bits, so 4294968676 becomes 1380 and passes the 68 to 9000 range check, while 99999999999999999999 becomes -1 and is rejected.
entries.rust_behavior: Reproduces the glibc result only: strtol-style saturation to the long range followed by truncation to i32, with no other undefined behavior. The same cases (opt_mtu_saturate_long_max, opt_mtu_wrap_u32_to_zero, opt_mtu_int_min_boundary) agree with C.

entries.title: Late probe reply enters the reorder stage
entries.c_behavior: Only the discovery loop treats probe-magic datagrams specially on the client. Outside discovery, a late or replayed authenticated probe reply (random value and counter both 2^64-1) is processed as ordinary data: its payload is written to the TUN device and it flips the reorder epoch, so the next real packet resets state again.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The inherited weakness is reproduced exactly and not fixed.
evidence: Packet too far ahead: expected 0, got 18446744073709551615
Random value mismatch - peer restarted. Resetting reorder state.

entries.title: reorder_init zeroes statistics on a window jump
entries.c_behavior: The too-far-ahead path adds the gap to packets_lost, then calls reorder_init, which zeroes every counter including packets_lost, so the loss total is always discarded. The statistics are never printed or exported, so only the reset path itself is externally visible.
entries.rust_behavior: The same reset runs and the same stderr line is printed. The statistics fields are kept and reset in the same order, and stay unobservable.
evidence: Packet too far ahead: expected 2, got 3000. Advancing window.

entries.title: Window test wraps near UINT64_MAX
entries.c_behavior: counter >= expected_counter + 1024 is evaluated in uint64_t. When expected_counter is within 1024 of UINT64_MAX the sum wraps to a small number, so every higher counter counts as 'too far ahead' and each one resets the window instead of being buffered.
entries.rust_behavior: Identical. The same wrapping unsigned arithmetic is used, so the same resets happen.
evidence: Packet too far ahead: expected 18446744073709551611, got 18446744073709551612

entries.title: First packet sets the baseline
entries.c_behavior: The first authenticated packet after start or reconnect sets expected_counter to its own counter, whatever it is, so a first counter of 1,000,000 (or 0, or 2^63) is delivered immediately and later lower counters count as old.

entries.title: Misleading ENOSPC in firewall errors
entries.c_behavior: shell_cmd sets errno to ENOSPC before it parses a command and never clears it, so a command that exits non-zero is reported as `Unable to run [...]: [No space left on device]`, and later perror calls with no failing call in between (for example tun_read on a zero-length read) print the same text.
entries.rust_behavior: errno is set to ENOSPC at the start of every command and the failure message reads the same text.
evidence: Unable to run [ip addr add $LOCAL_TUN_IP peer $REMOTE_TUN_IP dev $IF_NAME]: [No space left on device]

entries.title: Stale errno after a zero-length TUN read
entries.c_behavior: A zero-byte tun_read is treated as failure and perror prints whatever errno is left, which after the firewall setup is ENOSPC, so the line reads `tun_read: No space left on device`.
entries.rust_behavior: errno is left as ENOSPC by the command runner and perror prints the same text.
evidence: tun_read: No space left on device

entries.title: Event-loop failure still reports Done and exits 0
entries.c_behavior: A failure inside the event loop (a TUN read error, an exhausted client reconnect, a poll error) ends the loop, runs teardown, prints `Done.` and exits 0. Only setup failures exit non-zero.

entries.title: Tunnel IPv6 address is a text concatenation
entries.c_behavior: The IPv6 tunnel addresses are the text `64:ff9b::` followed by the IPv4 argument, so an IPv6 local or remote tunnel address yields an invalid string such as 64:ff9b::fd00::1 that is passed to ip unchanged.

entries.title: Gateway text is cut to 63 bytes
entries.c_behavior: The default-gateway text is read with fgets into a 64-byte buffer and stored in a 64-byte field, so an overlong gateway is cut to 63 bytes in `Gateway changed from [...] to [...]` messages.

entries.title: Key file may have trailing bytes
entries.c_behavior: Only the first 32 bytes of the key file are read, so a longer file is accepted and the extra bytes are ignored, while a shorter file is rejected.
evidence: Running in encrypted mode with authentication
